_comment: Runtime contracts, separate from the library ABI policy in
emu68k-bridge-policy.json. A contract is about the execution substrate -
processes, ports, signals, bindings, scheduling - which is hand-served
because it operates on GUEST memory the native OS cannot touch, and so has
A trace may PROPOSE a contract; only an entry here can change a status.
Every contract must be expressible without naming a program.

invariants: a created port names its creating task as owner
a created port owns an allocated signal bit, never bit zero by default
deleting a port releases the bit it names
only an explicitly bound destination may receive a pumped native message
a pumped message reaches exactly one guest destination
reply pairing is released exactly once
a process's own pr_MsgPort never receives native input
several windows may share one destination port
a context that never calls a blocking primitive must not starve its siblings
evidence_note: Observed: a child context polls a port tens of thousands of times and
never blocks, so a scheduler that only switches at Wait never resumes
the sibling that owns the input port. On real hardware preemption
hides this. The open question is which calls declare a yield;
a frame wait blocks until vertical blank on real hardware and is
therefore the first candidate.

invariants: identical input produces an identical OpenDevice result across repeated runs
a newly allocated slot is empty
a request is associated with exactly one live port
a failed open rolls back every native resource it took
a run that ends leaves no device open and no signal held
evidence_note: Observed: the same build opened keyboard.device successfully in one run
and failed in the next, with no input difference. An ordinary keyboard
open has no business alternating, and uninitialised request DATA cannot
explain the open itself changing outcome - only state carried across
opens can, so stale slot or request state is the first suspect, ahead of
leaked signals and cross-program runtime state.
Determinism must be settled BEFORE any command marshalling: an
intermittent open makes every result after it untrustworthy.
The matrix that separates the causes:
1. repeatedly after fresh boots      - is it per-boot state?
2. repeatedly within one instance    - is it per-run state?
3. alone vs after other programs     - is it cross-program state?
4. same and reversed open order      - is it slot reuse order?
What the trace has to carry to tell them apart: guest and native
IORequest addresses; unit, flags, request size, owning context; guest and
native reply ports with signal bit and signal task; slot index,
generation, previous state and each lifecycle transition; io_Device,
io_Unit and io_Error before and after the open; and the cleanup performed
on BOTH the success and the failure path.
